en: Vibhaṅga:
Analysis of the Faculties (Indriyavibhaṅga) 1.
Exposition according to the Abhidhamma (Abhidhammabhājanīya)
The twenty-two faculties: the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, the body faculty, the mind faculty, the female faculty, the male faculty, the life faculty,

the pleasure faculty, the pain faculty, the joy faculty, [the grief faculty, the equanimity faculty, the faith faculty, the energy faculty, the mindfulness faculty, the concentration faculty, the wisdom faculty, the I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown faculty, the final-knowledge faculty, and the final-knower faculty].
the faculty of mental displeasure, the faculty of equanimity, the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom,
the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of final knowledge, and the faculty of one who has already known.
In this context, what is the faculty of the eye?
That eye which is a sensitivity derived from the four great elements … [as above] … this empty village—
this is called the "eye-faculty.
Therein, what is the "ear-faculty" … [as above] …?
What is the nose faculty …pe… the tongue faculty …pe… the body faculty?
That body which is sensitivity derived from the four great elements ... [as above] ...
this empty village is called the "body faculty" (kāyindriya).
In that regard, what is the "mind faculty" (manindriya)?
The mind faculty is of one kind:
associated with contact.
The mind faculty is of two kinds:
There is that which is with root-cause; there is that which is without root-cause.
The mind-faculty is threefold:
there is the wholesome, there is the unwholesome, and there is the indeterminate.
The mind faculty is fourfold:

there is that belonging to the sense sphere, there is that belonging to the fine-material sphere, there is that belonging to the immaterial sphere, and there is that which is non-included (in the realms).
The mind faculty is fivefold: [there is that associated with each of the five types of consciousness].

There is that associated with the pleasure faculty; there is that associated with the pain faculty; there is that associated with the joy faculty; there is that associated with the grief faculty; there is that associated with the equanimity faculty.
The mind faculty is sixfold: eye-consciousness … pe … mind-consciousness.
Thus is the mind-faculty sixfold.
The mind-faculty is sevenfold:
eye-consciousness … [and so on] … body-consciousness, the mind-element, and the mind-consciousness-element.
Thus is the mind faculty in seven ways.
The mind faculty in eight ways:
eye-consciousness ... [and so on] ... body-consciousness; there is that accompanied by pleasure, there is that accompanied by pain, the mind element, and the mind-consciousness element.
Thus is the mind faculty by way of eightfold division.
The mind faculty by way of ninefold division:
eye-consciousness … pe … body-consciousness, the mind element, and the mind-consciousness element—which are wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
Thus is the mind faculty ninefold.
The mind faculty is tenfold:

there is eye-consciousness … pe … body-consciousness; there is that accompanied by pleasure, there is that accompanied by pain; the mind-element; and the mind-consciousness-element, which is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
Thus is the mind faculty in ten ways; ... [and so on] ...
thus is the mind faculty in many ways.
This is called "the mind faculty."
In this context, what is the female faculty (*itthindriya*)?
That which in a woman is the female characteristic, the female sign, the female deportment, the female appearance, the state of being female, the nature of being female—
this is called the "female faculty."
In this context, what is the male faculty (*purisindriya*)?
That which is the male characteristic, the male sign, the male deportment, the male appearance, the state of being male, and the nature of being male in a man—
this is called the "male faculty."
In this context, what is the life-faculty?
The life-faculty is twofold:
there is the material life-faculty and there is the immaterial life-faculty.
In this context, what is the material life faculty (*rūpajīvitindriya*)?
That which is the life-span, the persistence, the maintenance, the sustenance, the endurance, the continuance, the preservation, the vitality, and the life-faculty of those material phenomena—
this is called the "material life faculty."
In this context, what is the immaterial life-faculty?
That which is the life-span, the persistence, the maintenance, the upkeep, the endurance, the subsistence, the preservation, the life, and the life-faculty of those immaterial phenomena—
this is called the "immaterial life-faculty."
This is called the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
In this context, what is the pleasure-faculty (*sukhindriya*)?

That which is bodily satisfaction, bodily pleasure, the pleasant and pleasurable feeling born of body-contact, the pleasant and pleasurable sensation born of body-contact—this is [the pleasure-faculty].
This is called the faculty of pleasure (*sukhindriya*).
In that regard, what is the faculty of pain (*dukkhindriya*)?
That which is bodily displeasure, bodily pain, the unpleasant and painful feeling born of body-contact, the unpleasant and painful sensation born of body-contact—this is [the faculty of pain].
This is called the faculty of suffering (*dukkhindriya*).
In this context, what is the faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya*)?

It is that which is mental well-being, mental pleasure, the pleasant and happy feeling born of mental contact, the pleasant and happy sensation born of mental contact. This is the faculty of mental joy.
This is called the faculty of mental pleasure (*somanassindriya*).
In this context, what is the faculty of mental pain (*domanassindriya*)?
It is that which is mental unease, mental suffering, the unpleasant and painful feeling born of mental contact—the unpleasant and painful sensation born of mental contact.
This is called the faculty of mental displeasure (*domanassindriya*).
In this context, what is the faculty of equanimity (*upekkhindriya*)?

It is that mental state which is neither pleasant nor unpleasant, born of mental contact, a feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, and the sensation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure born of mental contact.
This is called the faculty of equanimity (*upekkhindriya*).
In this context, what is the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*)?
That which is faith, believing, conviction, serene confidence, faith, the faculty of faith, and the power of faith.
This is called the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*).
In this context, what is the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*)?
It is that which is mental exertion, the undertaking of energy, endeavor, striving, effort, perseverance, fortitude, steadfastness, stability, and firm resolve.
Unflagging perseverance, non-abandonment of zeal, non-abandonment of the burden, the exertion of the burden,
energy, the faculty of energy, the power of energy—
this is called the "faculty of energy."
In this context, what is the faculty of mindfulness?

That which is mindfulness, constant mindfulness, clear mindfulness, mindfulness, the state of being mindful, the state of bearing in mind, the state of not losing, the state of not forgetting, mindfulness, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, right mindfulness—
this is called the "faculty of mindfulness."
In this context, what is the faculty of concentration?

That which is the stability, steadfastness, firmness, non-distraction, and non-wavering of the mind; the state of having a mind that does not waver; serenity; the faculty of concentration; the power of concentration;
right concentration—this is called the "faculty of concentration."
Therein, what is the faculty of wisdom?
That which is wisdom, understanding ... [as before] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view—this is called the "faculty of wisdom."
In this context, what is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"?

It is the wisdom, the understanding, ... [as above] ... the absence of delusion, the investigation of phenomena, right view, the factor of enlightenment consisting of the investigation of phenomena, which pertains to the path and is included within the path, for the purpose of realizing those states that have not been known, not seen, not reached, not understood, and not realized.
This is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
In this context, what is the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*)?
It is the realization of those states that have been known, seen, attained, understood, and realized.
Wisdom, understanding … [as above] … non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, a factor of the path, included within the path—
this is called the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*). In this context, what is the faculty of one who has already known (*aññātāvindriya*)?

The wisdom, understanding, ... [and so on] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view, the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment, a factor of the path, included within the path, which pertains to those phenomena that have been known, seen, attained, realized, and verified for the sake of realization—this is called the "faculty of one who has already known."
The Exposition by Way of Categories (Abhidhammabhājanīya). 2.
The Interrogation (Pañhāpucchaka):
Twenty-two Faculties (Indriyāni).
The eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, the body faculty, the mind faculty, the female faculty,
the male faculty, the life faculty, the pleasure faculty, the pain faculty, the joy faculty,
the grief faculty, the equanimity faculty, the faith faculty, the energy faculty, the mindfulness faculty, and the concentration faculty.
The faculty of wisdom, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of final knowledge, and the faculty of one who has already known.
Of the twenty-two faculties, how many are wholesome, how many unwholesome, and how many indeterminate? ... [as above] ... How many are with conflict, and how many are without conflict? 2.1.
The Triads (Tika)
The eight faculties are indeterminate.
The faculty of mental displeasure is unwholesome.
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" is wholesome.
Four faculties may be wholesome, or they may be indeterminate.
Six faculties may be wholesome, may be unwholesome, or may be indeterminate.
Twelve faculties should not be said to be "associated with pleasant feeling," nor "associated with painful feeling," nor "associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."
Six faculties may be associated with pleasant feeling, or they may be associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Three faculties may be associated with pleasant feeling, may be associated with painful feeling, or may be associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The life-faculty may be associated with pleasant feeling, or it may be associated with painful feeling.

It may be associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; it may be such that it cannot be said to be associated with pleasant feeling, nor associated with painful feeling, nor associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Seven faculties are neither resultants nor subject to becoming resultants.
Three faculties are results of kamma.
Two faculties are subject to becoming results of kamma.
The faculty of final knowledge may be a result of kamma, or it may be subject to becoming a result of kamma.
Nine faculties may be resultants, may be subject to becoming resultants, or may be neither resultants nor subject to becoming resultants.
Nine faculties are acquired by clinging and are objects of clinging.
The faculty of mental grief is not acquired by clinging but is an object of clinging.
Three faculties are neither-clung-to-nor-liable-to-clinging.
Nine faculties may be both-clung-to-and-liable-to-clinging, may be neither-clung-to-yet-liable-to-clinging, or may be neither-clung-to-nor-liable-to-clinging.
Nine faculties are not-defiled-yet-defiling.
The faculty of displeasure is defiled and subject to defilement.
Three faculties are undefiled and not subject to defilement.
Three faculties may be undefiled but subject to defilement, or they may be undefiled and not subject to defilement.
Six faculties may be defiled and subject to defilement, may be undefiled but subject to defilement, or may be undefiled and not subject to defilement.
Nine faculties are without applied thought and without sustained thought.
The faculty of mental displeasure is with applied thought and with sustained thought.
The faculty of equanimity may be accompanied by initial application and sustained application, or it may be without initial application and without sustained application.

Eleven faculties may be accompanied by initial application and sustained application, or they may be without initial application and with sustained application only, or they may be without initial application and without sustained application.
Eleven faculties should not be described as "accompanied by rapture," nor as "accompanied by pleasure," nor as "accompanied by equanimity."

The faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya*) may be accompanied by rapture (*pītisahagata*), not accompanied by pleasure (*sukha*), and not accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*); or it may not be described as "accompanied by rapture.
Six faculties may be accompanied by rapture, may be accompanied by pleasure, or may be accompanied by equanimity.

Four faculties may be accompanied by rapture, may be accompanied by pleasure, or may be accompanied by equanimity; or they may not be described as "accompanied by rapture," nor as "accompanied by pleasure," nor as "accompanied by equanimity."
Fifteen faculties are neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation.
The faculty of mental displeasure may be abandoned by vision, or it may be abandoned by cultivation.
Six faculties may be abandoned by vision, may be abandoned by cultivation, or may be neither abandoned by vision nor by cultivation.
Fifteen faculties have roots that are neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation.
The faculty of mental displeasure may have roots to be abandoned by vision, or it may have roots to be abandoned by cultivation.
Six faculties may have roots to be abandoned by vision, may have roots to be abandoned by cultivation, or may have roots that are neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation.
These faculties neither lead to accumulation nor lead to diminution.
The faculty of mental displeasure leads to accumulation.
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" leads to diminution.
The faculty of final knowledge may be leading to diminution, or it may be neither leading to accumulation nor leading to diminution.
Nine faculties may be leading to accumulation, may be leading to diminution, or may be neither leading to accumulation nor leading to diminution.
Ten faculties are neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
The two faculties of those in training (sekha) are [training].
The faculty of one who has already known (aññātāvindriya) is beyond training (asekha).
Nine faculties may be of those in training, may be beyond training, or may be neither of those in training nor beyond training.
Six faculties are limited.
Three faculties are immeasurable.
Nine faculties may be limited, may be exalted, or may be immeasurable.
Seven faculties have no object.
Two faculties have limited objects.
Three faculties have immeasurable objects.

The faculty of displeasure may have a limited object, may have a sublime object, but does not have an immeasurable object; it may, however, not be described as having either a limited object or a sublime object.
Nine faculties may have a limited object, may have a sublime object, may have an immeasurable object, or may not be described as having a limited object, a sublime object, or an immeasurable object.
These nine faculties are intermediate.
The faculty of displeasure is inferior.
Three faculties are superior.
Three faculties may be intermediate or they may be superior.
Six faculties may be inferior, may be mediocre, or may be superior.
Ten faculties are undetermined.
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" is fixed in the rightness [of the path].
Four faculties may be fixed in the rightness [of liberation], or they may be unfixed.
The faculty of mental displeasure may be fixed in the wrongness [of bondage], or it may be unfixed.
Six faculties may be fixed in the wrongness, may be fixed in the rightness, or may be unfixed.
Seven faculties have no object.
Four faculties are not to be described as having the Path as their object, nor as having the Path as their cause, nor as having the Path as their predominance.

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" does not have the Path as its object; it may have the Path as its cause, it may have the Path as its predominance, or it may not be described as having the Path as its cause or as having the Path as its predominance.

The faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*) does not have the Path as its object; it may have the Path as its cause, it may have the Path as its predominance, or it may not be described as either "having the Path as its cause" or "having the Path as its predominance.

Nine faculties may have the Path as their object, may have the Path as their cause, may have the Path as their predominance, or they may not be described as "having the Path as their object," "having the Path as their cause," or "having the Path as their predominance.
Ten faculties may be arisen, may be bound to arise, but they are not to be described as "unarisen."
The two faculties may be arisen, may be unarisen, and should not be said to be "bound to arise.
Ten faculties may be arisen, may be unarisen, and may be bound to arise;
they may be past, may be future, and may be present.
Seven faculties have no object.
Two faculties have present objects.
Three faculties cannot be said to have either past objects, future objects, or present objects.
These faculties may have a past object, may have a future object, or may have a present object; or they may not be described as having a past object, nor a future object, nor a present object.
They may be internal, external, or both internal and external.
Seven faculties are without an object.
Three faculties have external objects.
Four faculties may have internal objects, may have external objects, or may have both internal and external objects.
Eight faculties may have internal objects, may have external objects, or may have both internal and external objects.
They may not be described as having an internal object, nor as having an external object, nor as having both an internal and external object.
Five faculties are non-demonstrable and impinging.
Seventeen faculties are non-demonstrable and non-impinging.
The Group on Roots (Hetugocchaka) Four faculties are roots.
Eighteen faculties are not roots.
Seven faculties are accompanied by roots.
Nine faculties are without roots.
Six faculties may be with root-cause, or they may be without root-cause.
Seven faculties are associated with root-causes.
Nine faculties are dissociated from root-causes.
Six faculties may be associated with roots, or they may be dissociated from roots.
Four faculties are both roots and accompanied by roots.
Nine faculties should not be described as "both roots and accompanied by roots," nor as "accompanied by roots but not roots."
Three faculties should not be described as “both roots and accompanied by roots.
They are accompanied by roots but are not roots.

Six faculties should not be described as “both roots and accompanied by roots”; they may be accompanied by roots but are not roots, or they may not be described as “accompanied by roots but are not roots.”
Four faculties are both roots and associated with roots.
Nine faculties should not be described as either "both roots and associated with roots" or "associated with roots but not roots.
Three faculties should not be described as "both roots and associated with roots," but they are associated with roots and are not roots.
Six faculties should not be said to be "both roots and associated with roots"; they may be associated with roots but not roots, or they may not be said to be "associated with roots but not roots.
Nine faculties are not roots and are rootless.
Three faculties are not roots but are accompanied by roots.
The four faculties are not to be described as "not roots but accompanied by roots," nor as "not roots and rootless.
Six faculties may be "not roots but accompanied by roots," and they may be "not roots and rootless.
2.2.2. The Short Intermediate Pair (Cūḷantaraduka).
With conditions.
Conditioned.
Non-manifesting.
Five faculties are with resistance.
Seventeen faculties are without resistance.
Seven faculties are material.
Fourteen faculties are immaterial.
The life-faculty may be material or it may be immaterial.
Ten faculties are mundane.
Three faculties are supramundane.
Nine faculties may be mundane or supramundane;
they may be cognizable by some, or not cognizable by some.
2.2.3. Group on the Taints (Āsavagocchaka) There are no taints (āsava).
Ten faculties (indriya) are associated with taints (sāsava).
Three faculties are without taints (*anāsava*).
Nine faculties may be with taints (*sāsava*) or without taints.
Fifteen faculties are dissociated from the taints.
The faculty of displeasure is associated with the taints (*āsava*).
Six faculties may be either associated with the taints or dissociated from the taints.
Ten faculties should not be described as "both taints and subject to the taints," but rather as "subject to the taints and not themselves taints."
Three faculties should not be described as “both taints and associated with taints,” nor as “associated with taints but not taints.

Nine faculties should not be described as “both taints and associated with taints”; they may be “associated with taints but not taints,” or they may not be described as “associated with taints but not taints.
Fifteen faculties should not be described as “both taints and associated with taints,” nor as “associated with taints but not taints.”

The faculty of displeasure (*domanassindriya*) should not be said to be "both an outflow (*āsava*) and associated with an outflow"; rather, it is associated with an outflow but is not itself an outflow.

Six faculties should not be said to be "both outflows and associated with outflows"; they may be associated with outflows but are not themselves outflows, or they may not be said to be "associated with outflows but are not themselves outflows.
Nine faculties are dissociated from outflows yet possess outflows (*sāsava*).
Three faculties are dissociated from the taints and are without taints (*anāsava*).
The faculty of mental displeasure (*domanassindriya*) should not be said to be either "dissociated from the taints and with taints" or "dissociated from the taints and without taints.
Three faculties may be either dissociated from the taints and with taints, or dissociated from the taints and without taints.

Six faculties may be dissociated from the taints and subject to taints; they may be dissociated from the taints and free from taints; or they may not be described as either "dissociated from the taints and subject to taints" or "dissociated from the taints and free from taints.
2.2.4. The Group on Fetters (Saṃyojana-gocchaka):
They are not fetters.
Six faculties are subject to fetters.
Three faculties are not subject to fetters.
Nine faculties may be subject to fetters, or they may not be subject to fetters.
Fifteen faculties are dissociated from the fetters.
The faculty of mental displeasure is associated with the fetters.
Six faculties may be either associated with the fetters or dissociated from the fetters.
The ten faculties cannot be described as "both fetters and objects of the fetters"; they are objects of the fetters but are not themselves fetters.
Three faculties cannot be described either as "both fetters and objects of the fetters" or as "objects of the fetters but not themselves fetters.

Nine faculties cannot be described as "both fetters and objects of the fetters"; they may be objects of the fetters but not themselves fetters, or they may not be described as "objects of the fetters but not themselves fetters."
The fifteen faculties should not be described as "both fetters and associated with fetters," nor as "associated with fetters but not fetters.
The faculty of mental grief should not be described as "both a fetter and associated with fetters," but it is "associated with fetters but not a fetter."

Six faculties should not be described as "both fetters and associated with fetters"; they may be associated with fetters but are not themselves fetters, or they may not be described as "associated with fetters but are not themselves fetters.
Nine faculties are dissociated from fetters but are subject to fetters (*saṃyojaniya*).
Three faculties are dissociated from fetters and are not subject to fetters.
The faculty of displeasure (domanassindriya) should not be described as either "dissociated from the fetters and subject to fettering" or "dissociated from the fetters and not subject to fettering.
Three faculties may be dissociated from the fetters and subject to fettering, or they may be dissociated from the fetters and not subject to fettering.

Six faculties may be dissociated from the fetters and subject to fettering, or they may be dissociated from the fetters and not subject to fettering, or they should not be described as either "dissociated from the fetters and subject to fettering" or "dissociated from the fetters and not subject to fettering."
2.2.5. Group on the Fetter (Ganthagocchaka).
There are no fetters.
Ten faculties are objects of the fetters.
Three faculties are not objects of the fetters.
Nine faculties may be objects of the fetters, or they may not be objects of the fetters.
Fifteen faculties are dissociated from the fetters.
The faculty of displeasure is associated with the ties (*gantha*).
Six faculties may be either associated with the ties or dissociated from the ties.
Ten faculties should not be said to be "both ties and objects of the ties," but rather they are "objects of the ties but not themselves ties."
Three faculties should not be described as either "fetters and objects of the fetters" or "objects of the fetters but not fetters.

Nine faculties should not be described as "fetters and objects of the fetters"; they may be "objects of the fetters but not fetters," or they may not be described as "objects of the fetters but not fetters.
Fifteen faculties should not be described as either "fetters and associated with the fetters" or "associated with the fetters but not fetters."
The faculty of displeasure (*domanassindriya*) should not be said to be "both a tie (*gantha*) and associated with ties"; rather, it is associated with ties but is not itself a tie.

Six faculties should not be said to be "both ties and associated with ties"; they may be associated with ties but not themselves ties, or they may not be said to be "associated with ties but not themselves ties.
Nine faculties are dissociated from ties and are subject to ties (*ganthavippayutta-ganthaniya*).
Three faculties are dissociated from the fetters and are not subject to the fetters.
The faculty of mental displeasure should not be said to be either “dissociated from the fetters and subject to the fetters” or “dissociated from the fetters and not subject to the fetters.
Three faculties may be dissociated from the fetters and subject to the fetters, or they may be dissociated from the fetters and not subject to the fetters.

Six faculties may be dissociated from the ties and subject to the ties; they may be dissociated from the ties and not subject to the ties; they may not be described as either "dissociated from the ties and subject to the ties" or "dissociated from the ties and not subject to the ties.
5.2.2.6. The Group on Floods, Yokes, and Hindrances: [The six faculties] are not floods... [and so forth].
There are no yogas ...
[and so on] ... no hindrances.
Ten faculties are subject to hindrance.
Three faculties are not associated with the hindrances.
Nine faculties may be associated with the hindrances, or they may not be associated with the hindrances.
Fifteen faculties are dissociated from the hindrances.
The faculty of mental displeasure (*domanassindriya*) is associated with the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
Six faculties may be associated with the hindrances, or they may be dissociated from the hindrances.
Ten faculties should not be described as "both hindrances and objects of the hindrances," but rather as "objects of the hindrances but not hindrances."
Three faculties should not be described as either "both hindrances and objects of hindrance" or "objects of hindrance but not hindrances.

Nine faculties should not be described as "both hindrances and objects of hindrance"; they may be "objects of hindrance but not hindrances," or they may not be described as "objects of hindrance but not hindrances.
Fifteen faculties should not be described as either "both hindrances and associated with hindrances" or "associated with hindrances but not hindrances."

The faculty of displeasure (*domanassindriya*) should not be said to be "both an hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*) and associated with an hindrance"; rather, it is associated with an hindrance but is not itself an hindrance.

Six faculties should not be said to be "both hindrances and associated with hindrances"; they may be associated with hindrances but are not themselves hindrances, or they should not be said to be "associated with hindrances but are not themselves hindrances.
Nine faculties are dissociated from hindrances and are subject to hindrances (*nīvaraṇiya*).
Three faculties are dissociated from the hindrances and are non-hindrance-factors.
The faculty of mental displeasure should not be described as either "dissociated from the hindrances and a hindrance-factor" or "dissociated from the hindrances and a non-hindrance-factor.
Three faculties may be either dissociated from the hindrances and hindrance-factors, or dissociated from the hindrances and non-hindrance-factors.

Six faculties may be dissociated from the hindrances and subject to the hindrances; they may be dissociated from the hindrances and not subject to the hindrances; or they may not be described as either "dissociated from the hindrances and subject to the hindrances" or "dissociated from the hindrances and not subject to the hindrances.
2.2.9. The Group on Misapprehension (Parāmāsa-gocchaka):
None are misapprehensions.
Six faculties are associated with clinging.
Three faculties are not associated with clinging.
Nine faculties may be associated with clinging, or they may not be associated with clinging.
Sixteen faculties are dissociated from the perversions.
Six faculties may be associated with the perversions, and may be dissociated from the perversions.
Ten faculties should not be said to be "both perversions and objects of perversion"; they are objects of perversion but are not themselves perversions.
Three faculties should not be described as "both corruptions and corrupted," nor as "corrupted but not corruptions.
Nine faculties should not be described as "both corruptions and corrupted"; they may be "corrupted but not corruptions," or they may not be described as "corrupted but not corruptions.
Ten faculties are dissociated from corruption yet corrupted.
Three faculties are dissociated from and unattached to the perversions (*parāmāsa*).
Three faculties may be dissociated from the perversions and attached to them, or they may be dissociated from the perversions and unattached to them.
